data.text:
A Spark of Hope at the People’s Monument

Today, on Martial Law Day, I joined fellow citizens at the People’s Monument in Quezon City—just a short walk from home. I was invited to speak elsewhere, but something told me to stay close. I’m grateful I did.

Despite the rain and traffic, people kept coming. Old friends, social media kindred spirits, distinguished leaders, and everyday Filipinos—braving the weather and the risks, not for spectacle, but to speak truth, to be heard, to remember. I stayed for two hours, listening to the crowd, watching the quiet courage of those who refused to be silenced.

And in that sea of voices, I met someone extraordinary: Francis Joseph “Kiko” Aquino Dee. He thanked me for mentioning him in my posts—but truly, it is I who should thank him.

Kiko is not one to seek the spotlight, though it often finds him. A writer, educator, and political analyst, he has quietly built a reputation for thoughtful commentary and principled leadership. He teaches at the University of the Philippines and contributes to Rappler, where his essays reflect both intellectual depth and moral clarity. He studied Political Science at UP Diliman and earned his Master’s in Political Economy from the London School of Economics.

But beyond credentials, what struck me most was his humility. He carries the legacy of the Aquino and Dee families—names etched in our nation’s history—but he walks his own path with grace. His voice is calm, his convictions firm. He speaks not to impress, but to awaken.

Today, he served as spokesperson for the “Trillion Peso March”—a movement born of conscience, not ambition. And he did so with quiet dignity, reminding us that leadership is not about volume, but about values.

I told him to keep going. To continue inspiring. Because we need young leaders like Kiko—those who can communicate with heart, mobilize with wisdom, and lead with soul.

This rally was more than a protest. It was a reunion of conscience. A reminder that we are not alone. That we are still fighting—for our rights, for truth, for justice. May this day remind us that silence is never an option, and that the rain cannot wash away our resolve.

To Kiko, and to every young Filipino who dares to speak up: we see you. We believe in you. And we walk beside you.

#RelentlessForChange

data.text:
Thousands Rally Across Philippines in Anti-Corruption Protests..

#Manila #Philippines: Massive protests erupted across the Philippines on Sunday, as thousands of demonstrators filled the streets of Manila and several major cities to denounce corruption and demand government accountability.
At the heart of the capital, large crowds gathered near Ayala Bridge and Mendiola, where tensions rose as protesters clashed with police. Witnesses reported that some demonstrators hurled rocks and set a truck ablaze, while security forces responded with crowd dispersal measures.
The Philippine National Police (PNP) said they exercised maximum tolerance during the commotion, but confirmed that at least 17 protesters were arrested and around 30 police officers sustained injuries.
Despite the confrontations, rallies remained largely peaceful in other cities, with civic groups, students, and religious organizations joining calls for greater transparency in government spending.
Organizers vowed to continue demonstrations in the coming weeks, framing the protests as part of a broader movement to confront what they describe as systemic corruption undermining public trust.

data.text:
🇵🇭 It's hot in the Philippines: people took to the streets

In Rizal Park in Manila on September 21, more than 13,000 protesters took to the streets to express dissatisfaction with corrupt officials. The unrest began due to a corruption scandal involving fake flood control projects that cost taxpayers billions of dollars. Earlier, House Speaker Martin Romualdez, a cousin of Philippine President Marcos, resigned due to his involvement in this scandal.

The Philippine military declared a "red alert" level. According to protest organizers, more than 30,000 people are expected to participate in the protest on EDSA Boulevard in Manila. EDSA is the main street of Manila, where Filipinos held a protest march in 1986.

Earlier this month, a construction company accused nearly 30 members of the House of Representatives and officials from the Department of Public Works and Highways of accepting bribes, which caused widespread public outrage. Philippine President Marcos announced the creation of an independent agency to investigate cases of illegal appropriation and embezzlement of funds allocated for flood control. According to AFP, the Philippine Department of Finance estimates that corruption in flood control projects will cost the country's economy 118.5 billion pesos ($2 billion) from 2023 to 2025.
